text: అవును. పక్షులు [[theropod|థెరోపాడ్‌లు]] అనే డైనోసార్ల గుంపుకు చెందినవే. టి. రెక్స్, [[@velociraptor-real|వెలోసిరాప్టర్]] ఉన్నదీ ఇదే గుంపు.

విష్‌బోన్ నుంచి కొన్ని డైనోసార్లు [[@wild-penguin-dads|గూటి మీద పొదిగిన]] తీరు వరకూ, శాస్త్రవేత్తలు డజన్ల కొద్దీ పోలికలను సరిపోల్చారు. చైనాలో దొరికిన ఈకల [[fossil|శిలాజాలు]], జంతువుల మధ్య బంధుత్వం మీద చేసిన పరిశోధనలు, అన్నీ ఒకే వైపు చూపిస్తున్నాయి.

అంటే డైనోసార్లు పూర్తిగా అంతరించిపోలేదు. 6.6 కోట్ల ఏళ్ల క్రితం [[@extinction|గ్రహశకలం]] ఢీకొన్నప్పుడు, ఈకలున్న ఒక చిన్న కొమ్మ ప్రాణాలతో బయటపడింది. అది ఇప్పటికీ మన మధ్యే ఉంది. ఈ రోజు సుమారు 11,000 రకాల పక్షులు బతికి ఉన్నాయి. అంటే ఇప్పుడు [[mammal|క్షీరదాల]] రకాల కంటే డైనోసార్ల రకాలే ఎక్కువ.

traits.d: రెండింటికీ విష్‌బోన్ ఉంటుంది. రెండు కాలర్ ఎముకలు (భుజాన్ని ఛాతీకి కలిపే ఎముకలు) కలిసి స్ప్రింగులా వంగే V ఆకారం.
రెండింటి ఎముకల్లోనూ లోపల గాలి ఖాళీలు ఉంటాయి. అవి ఊపిరి పీల్చడానికి సాయపడే గాలి సంచులకు కలుస్తాయి.
మాంసం తినే చాలా డైనోసార్లకు ఈకలు ఉండేవి. పక్షులు వాటిని అలాగే ఉంచుకున్నాయి.
కోడి కాలు చూడు. తర్వాత డైనోసార్ అడుగుజాడ చూడు. రెండిటిదీ ఒకటే నమూనా.
ఒవిరాప్టర్ లాంటి డైనోసార్లు కోడిపెట్టలా చేతులు చాపి గుడ్ల మీద కూర్చున్నట్టు శిలాజాలు చూపిస్తున్నాయి.

sec.t:
1861లో జర్మనీలో ఒక క్వారీలో పనిచేసేవాళ్లకు ఆర్కియోప్టెరిక్స్ (Archaeopteryx) దొరికింది. ఒకప్పుడు ఒక మడుగు అడుగున ఉన్న బురదే గట్టిపడి ఏర్పడిన మెత్తని సున్నపురాయిలో అది ఉంది. దాని సైజు దాదాపు కాకి అంత. పక్షిలా ఈకలు, రెక్కలు ఉన్నాయి. కానీ డైనోసార్‌లా పళ్లు, గోళ్లున్న వేళ్లు, ఎముకలతో పొడవాటి తోక కూడా ఉన్నాయి. రెండిటికీ మధ్యలో ఉండే జీవికి సరైన ఉదాహరణలా కనిపించింది.

దానికి రెండేళ్ల ముందే చార్లెస్ డార్విన్ [[evolution|పరిణామం]] మీద తన పుస్తకాన్ని ప్రచురించాడు. సమయం భలే కుదిరింది. కొన్నేళ్ల తర్వాత ఇంగ్లిష్ శాస్త్రవేత్త థామస్ హెన్రీ హక్స్‌లీ ఒక విషయం గమనించాడు. ఆర్కియోప్టెరిక్స్ కాంప్సోగ్నేథస్ అనే చిన్న డైనోసార్‌ను చాలా పోలి ఉంది. పక్షులకూ డైనోసార్లకూ బంధుత్వం ఉందని ఆయన సూచించాడు. కానీ ఆ తర్వాత దాదాపు వందేళ్ల పాటు ఆ ఆలోచనను ఎవరూ పెద్దగా పట్టించుకోలేదు.

1970లలో అమెరికన్ శాస్త్రవేత్త జాన్ ఆస్ట్రమ్ ఆర్కియోప్టెరిక్స్‌ను డైనోనికస్ అనే చిన్న వేటగాడితో పోల్చి, హక్స్‌లీ ఆలోచనకు మళ్లీ ప్రాణం పోశాడు. తర్వాత 1996లో చైనాలోని లియావోనింగ్‌లో ఒక రైతుకు సైనోసారాప్టెరిక్స్ అనే చిన్న డైనోసార్ దొరికింది. దాని ఒంటి మీద మెత్తటి నూగు లాంటి పోగులు ఉన్నాయి. ఈకల లాంటి కప్పుతో దొరికిన మొదటి పక్షి కాని డైనోసార్ అదే.

అప్పటి నుంచి వందల కొద్దీ ఈకల డైనోసార్లు దొరికాయి, ముఖ్యంగా చైనాలో. కొన్నిటికి కేవలం నూగు ఉండేది. మరికొన్నిటికి పూర్తి రెక్కలు. మైక్రోరాప్టర్‌కు చేతుల మీదా కాళ్ల మీదా పొడవాటి ఈకలు ఉండేవి. నాలుగు రెక్కల పాతకాలపు విమానంలా. [[@feathers|ఎగరడం కంటే చాలా ముందే ఈకలు వచ్చాయి]].

[[@space-asteroid-defence|గ్రహశకలం ఢీకొన్నప్పుడు]] దాదాపు అన్ని డైనోసార్లూ చనిపోయాయి. కొన్ని పక్షులు మాత్రమే బతికాయి. అడవులు కూలిపోయినప్పుడు గింజలు తిని బతకగలిగే, ముక్కులున్న, నేల మీద తిరిగే చిన్న పక్షులే బతికి ఉంటాయని చాలా మంది శాస్త్రవేత్తల అభిప్రాయం. చెట్ల మీద ఉండే పక్షులు, పళ్లున్న పక్షులు బతకలేకపోయాయి.

అంతరించిపోయిన వాటిని శాస్త్రవేత్తలు ‘పక్షులు కాని డైనోసార్లు’ అంటారు. పక్షులు ‘పక్షి డైనోసార్లు’. అంటే కాకులు, [[@pigeons-homing|పావురాలు]], నెమళ్లు అన్నీ డైనోసార్లే. వాటిలో [[@crow-smart|కొన్ని మహా తెలివైనవి]]. డైనోసార్లు కాని వాటిలో వాటికి అతి దగ్గరి బంధువులు [[@croc-ancient|మొసళ్లు, ఎలిగేటర్లు]]. అవి కూడా గూళ్లు కడతాయి, పిల్లలను పిలుస్తాయి.

భారతదేశ జాతీయ పక్షి నెమలి, అమెరికా జాతీయ పక్షి [[@bald-eagle|బట్టతల గద్ద]], రెండూ థెరోపాడ్ డైనోసార్లే. ముందుకు మూడు వేళ్లు, వంకర తిరిగిన పదునైన గోళ్లు ఉండే [[@eagles-hunt|గద్ద పాదం]], డైనోసార్ల కాలంలో మూడు వేళ్ల అడుగుజాడలు వదిలిన పాదాల నమూనాలోనే ఉంటుంది. బతికున్న పక్షుల్లో అతి పెద్దదైన [[@penguin-flight|నిప్పుకోడి]] పొలుసుల పొడవాటి కాళ్లతో గంటకు సుమారు 70 కి.మీ. వేగంతో పరిగెడుతుంది. ఆ కాళ్లు ఒక చిన్న డైనోసార్‌కు అతికించినా తేడా తెలియదు. కిటికీ మీద గెంతే పిచ్చుక కూడా ఈ కుటుంబంలో భాగమే.

text: The deepest hole people have ever made is the Kola Superdeep Borehole, in the far north-west of Russia, near the border with Norway. Soviet scientists started drilling in 1970. By 1989, they had reached 12,262 m, about 12 km straight down. That's deeper than [[@mountains-tallest|Mount Everest]] is tall, by more than 3 km.

But it's not a hole you could climb into. At the bottom, it's only about 23 cm wide, narrower than a dinner plate. The drilling stopped because the rock got too hot. Today the top is sealed with a rusty metal cap.

They heard strange sounds and got scared
They hit the Earth's mantle

st.reveal: At the bottom, the rock was about 180 °C, much hotter than the roughly 100 °C scientists had predicted. The hot rock flowed slowly and kept clogging the hole, and the drill equipment couldn't cope.

myth: Scientists drilling in the Kola hole recorded the screams of people in hell.

This was a hoax that spread through radio shows and newsletters around 1989 and 1990, and later online. The "recording" was taken from a horror film soundtrack. The Kola scientists never reported any such thing.

sec.t:
The Kola project wasn't about oil or gold. It was pure science. During the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], the Soviet Union and the USA competed in space and also in reaching deep inside Earth. American scientists had tried a deep-sea drilling project called Project Mohole in the 1960s, but it was cancelled.

The Soviets wanted to drill through the crust, the Earth's outer skin, and learn what it was really made of. Nobody had ever seen rock from so far down. [[geologist|Geologists]] had theories from studying earthquake waves, but they wanted real samples.

Drilling that deep was slow, hard work. Instead of spinning the whole 12 km string of pipe, the team used a [[turbine|turbine]] at the bottom, driven by mud pumped down the pipe, to turn the drill bit. Every time a bit wore out, the entire pipe had to be hauled up and taken apart, section by section, which could take many hours.

Some oil wells are longer than Kola. In 2011, the Z-44 Chayvo well near Sakhalin Island in Russia reached about 12,345 m. But oil wells often curve sideways through the rock to reach oil, so they're long without going as deep.

In 2025, China finished Shenditake 1, a vertical well in the Taklamakan Desert. It reached 10,910 m, the deepest in Asia, though still short of Kola.

For deep places people can actually visit, the record holders are mines. The Mponeng gold mine in South Africa goes about 4 km down, and miners need powerful cooling to cope with rock hot enough to burn skin.

Earth's centre is about 6,371 km below your feet. So the Kola hole is just 0.2% of the way there. If Earth were an apple, the hole wouldn't even get through the skin.

The crust under continents is usually 30 to 50 km thick, so Kola didn't come close to the mantle underneath. Scientists still learn about deep Earth mainly by studying how earthquake waves bend and bounce. Under Indian cities, many [[@wells-borewells|borewells]] go down a few hundred metres to find water, which is nothing compared with Kola, but enough to drain old [[aquifer|aquifers]]. Physicists have even worked out what would happen if a hole went all the way, and the answer, in [[@what-if-hole-through-earth|a hole through the Earth]], involves a fall lasting roughly 40 minutes.

text: Coal, oil and [[@earth-weird-door-to-hell|natural gas]] are called [[fossil|fossil]] fuels, because they are made from things that lived long ago. Coal is the squashed remains of ancient plants. Oil and gas come mostly from tiny sea creatures.

In both cases, dead living things were buried before they could rot away. Layer after layer of mud and sand piled on top. Deep underground, heat and pressure slowly changed them over millions of years. When we burn them, we release energy that those plants and [[plankton|plankton]] first captured from sunlight.

Dinosaurs

st.reveal: Mostly microscopic sea life. Over millions of years, trillions of dead plankton and algae sank to the sea floor, got buried in mud, and were slowly cooked by Earth's heat into oil and gas. Trees made coal instead.

That squashing is the first step in turning plants into coal. Nature just adds far more weight and millions of years.
myth: Oil comes from dead dinosaurs.

Almost none of it does. Most oil formed from tiny ocean plankton and algae, and much of it is older or younger than the dinosaurs. Coal comes from plants. The dinosaur idea was helped along by old advertising.

sec.t:
About 300 to 360 million years ago, during a time called the Carboniferous, much of the land was covered in warm swamps. Giant ferns and tree-sized relatives of today's little horsetail plants grew there. When they died, they fell into still water with little oxygen, so they didn't rot completely. They piled up as a soggy brown mass called peat.

As more mud buried the peat, it was squeezed and heated. Water and gases were pressed out. Peat became soft brown coal, called lignite, then harder black coal. It takes many metres of plants to make one metre of coal.

India's coal is a bit younger. Most formed around 250 to 300 million years ago, when India was part of [[gondwana|Gondwana]], joined to [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] and Africa. The same kinds of fossil leaves turn up in coal on all those continents, one of the clues that [[@india-drift|India drifted]] across the planet.

{{story:industrial-revolution}}

Oil has a different recipe. Oceans are full of plankton, living things so small you need a [[microscope|microscope]] to see them. When they die, many sink and settle in mud on the sea floor.

If that mud gets buried deep, it heats up. Between about 60 and 120 °C, the remains slowly break down into oil. Hotter still, they turn into natural gas. Oil and gas are lighter than water, so they creep upwards through rock until something stops them, such as a layer of tight rock like a lid. That's where drillers look.

In 1859, Edwin Drake drilled a well at Titusville, Pennsylvania, and struck oil about 21 m down. It started the modern oil industry. In India, oil was found at Digboi in Assam in 1889, and its refinery, opened in 1901, is one of the oldest still working anywhere. In 1974, drillers working from a rig called Sagar Samrat struck a huge oilfield under the Arabian Sea, about 170 km off Mumbai. Named Bombay High, it is still India's largest oilfield, pumped from platforms standing in the open sea.

Coal powered the [[@steam-engine|steam engines]] of the Industrial Revolution, and it still makes most of India's [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. Oil gives us petrol, diesel and jet fuel. It is also the starting point for most [[@plastic-made|plastics]], and even some paints, medicines and clothing.

Fossil fuels took millions of years to form, and we are using them up in a few centuries. Burning them releases [[@carbon-cycle|carbon dioxide]] that was locked away underground, which is the main cause of [[@climate-change|climate change]]. It also makes smoke that dirties the air.

That's why countries are building more [[@renewable-energy|solar and wind power]]. Coal mining has left its own marks too. In Jharia, fires that started in underground coal seams more than a century ago still smoulder beneath towns and roads.

text: A dwarf planet is a world that [[orbit|orbits]] the Sun and is big enough for its own [[gravity|gravity]] to pull it into a round shape. But it hasn't cleared other objects out of its path. That last rule is what separates it from the [[@planets-order|eight planets]].

The International Astronomical Union (IAU), which names objects in space, created this category in 2006. Five dwarf planets are officially recognised: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. Ceres lives in the [[asteroidbelt|asteroid belt]] between Mars and Jupiter. The other four orbit beyond [[@neptune-winds|Neptune]], among the icy bodies of the [[@kuiper-belt|Kuiper Belt]] and further out.
[[astronomer|Astronomers]] think there could be many more, perhaps over a hundred, still waiting to be studied or officially counted.

st.prompt: Under the 2006 rules, why isn't Pluto a full planet?

options.t: It hasn't cleared other objects out of its path around the Sun
It isn't round

st.reveal: Pluto orbits the Sun and is round, so it passes the first two tests. But it shares its region with thousands of other icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt. The eight planets are each the biggest thing by far in their own lanes.

n.certNote: The International Astronomical Union's 2006 definition is the official one. Many planetary scientists think it is a poor definition, and they disagree about how many dwarf planets there are.

sec.h: Ceres, the planet that kept changing
sec.t:
On 1 January 1801, the Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi found a small object orbiting between Mars and Jupiter. It was named Ceres, after the Roman goddess of farming, and was called a planet. Then astronomers found more and more objects in the same region. By the 1850s, they had a new name for them all: [[asteroid|asteroids]].

In 2006, Ceres was promoted to dwarf planet, because it is round. It is about 940 km across, a little less than the road trip from Delhi to Ahmedabad. NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited it from 2015 to 2018 and found bright white spots inside a [[crater|crater]]. They turned out to be salts left behind by salty water that seeped up from below.

sec.h: The world that started the argument
sec.t:
In 2005, a team led by the American astronomer Mike Brown found a distant world that seemed bigger than Pluto. It was named Eris, after the Greek goddess of strife and discord, a fitting name from the [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]] given the fight that followed.

If Pluto was a planet, Eris had to be one too, and there were probably dozens more like them. Astronomers had to choose between a [[solar-system|solar system]] with dozens of planets and a new definition. At a meeting in Prague in 2006, IAU members voted for the new rules, and [[@pluto|Pluto]] became a dwarf planet.

Later measurements showed Pluto is slightly wider than Eris, but Eris is about a quarter heavier.

{{story:easter-island}}

Haumea spins so fast, once every four hours or so, that it has stretched into an egg or rugby-ball shape. In 2017, astronomers found it has a thin ring. It is named after Haumea, a goddess of birth in [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaiian]] tradition, since telescopes on Hawaii helped study it and its two small moons.

Makemake is named after the creator god of the people of Rapa Nui, also called [[@easter-island|Easter Island]]. It was found shortly after Easter in 2005. Its surface is coated with frozen methane.

Other big icy bodies, such as Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna and Orcus, may also be round enough to qualify. Some astronomers already call them dwarf planets, while the IAU has not formally added them.

Many planetary scientists dislike the 2006 definition. Only a few hundred astronomers voted, out of thousands of IAU members, because the vote was held on the last day of the meeting. Critics also say that "clearing the orbit" is vague, since even Earth shares its path with some asteroids.

Alan Stern, who leads NASA's New Horizons mission to Pluto, argues that anything round enough should count as a planet. That would make the solar system home to well over a hundred planets. Others say a clear dividing line is useful, even if it isn't perfect. Students in India and the USA learn the same answer for now: eight planets and a growing family of dwarfs.

text: Nobody can dig a hole through the Earth. The planet is about 12,742 kilometres across, and the deepest hole ever drilled reached just over 12 kilometres. Beyond that, rocks get too hot and squeezed for any drill to work. At the centre, the temperature is around 5,000 to 6,000 °C, about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

But physicists love this question, because it shows how [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] works. If somehow there were a tunnel straight through the middle, with no air and walls that didn't melt, you could jump in and fall all the way through. You'd zoom past the centre at roughly 8 to 10 kilometres a second and reach the far side about 38 minutes later.

st.prompt: If you fell down a hole through the Earth with no air to slow you, what would happen when you reached the other side?

options.t: You'd slow to a stop right at the far surface, then fall back again
You'd shoot out high into space
You'd get stuck floating at the centre straight away

st.reveal: You'd speed up all the way to the centre, then slow down as gravity pulled you back. With no air, you'd just reach the far side, stop for a moment, then fall all the way back. Back and forth for ever, like a giant swing.

src: Klotz A. (2015), The gravity tunnel in a non-uniform Earth, American Journal of Physics.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kola Superdeep Borehole.
n.certNote: The fall times come from real physics, but they assume a tunnel with no air and walls that don't melt, which is impossible. Nobody has drilled more than about 12 km down, so the deep Earth is known only from earthquake waves and lab experiments.

sec.t:
In 1970 scientists in the Soviet Union began drilling into the Kola Peninsula, near the Arctic. They kept going for about 20 years. In 1989 the hole reached 12,262 metres, the [[@extreme-deepest-hole|deepest hole]] ever made, but only about 23 centimetres wide.

At the bottom, the rock was about 180 °C, far hotter than expected. It became soft and gooey, closing in around the drill. The project stopped. Even this record barely scratched the Earth's crust, the thin outer shell, which under the continents is usually about 30 to 50 kilometres thick.

For years, textbooks said the fall would take about 42 minutes. That assumed the Earth was the same all the way through. In 2015 a physics student named Alexander Klotz redid the sum using what we actually know about the inside of the Earth.

The [[core|core]] is made mostly of iron and nickel and is much denser than the rocks near the surface. That extra mass at the centre means gravity stays strong deeper down, so you'd pick up speed faster. His answer was about 38 minutes, roughly as long as a school lesson.

Real life would ruin the trip in many ways. Air in the tunnel would slow you to about the speed of a skydiver, and the fall would take days, not minutes. The [[mantle|mantle]] rock would be hot enough to glow. The outer core is liquid metal, swirling like a slow ocean. Pressure at the centre is more than three million times the air pressure you feel now.

The Earth's spin also causes trouble. A tunnel from pole to pole would work best. Anywhere else, the planet's rotation would push you sideways into the walls as you fell.

The point exactly opposite you on the globe is called your antipode. Most land on Earth has ocean on the other side, because about 71 percent of the planet's surface is water.

Dig down from Delhi or Bengaluru and you'd surface in the Pacific Ocean, far west of Chile or Peru. Start in Kansas and you'd pop up in the Indian Ocean, southwest of Australia. China's opposite point is mostly in Argentina and Chile. And the strangest part? Even at the centre, you'd never escape Earth's grip, because leaving it takes a very different kind of speed, called [[@how-escape-velocity|escape velocity]].

text: Sea otters [[@sleep-why|sleep]] floating on their backs in the sea. Waves and currents could easily carry a sleeping otter away from its group. So otters sometimes hold paws while they snooze, or wrap themselves in long ribbons of seaweed called kelp, which is anchored to the seabed.
Groups of floating otters are called rafts. Some rafts are just a handful of otters. Others have dozens, or even hundreds, bobbing together like a floating mat.
Mothers and pups stay especially close. A pup sleeps on its mother's belly, and when she dives for food, she may tie it up in kelp so it can't float off.

sec.t:
Most sea [[mammal|mammals]], like seals and whales, stay warm with thick blubber. Sea otters have hardly any. Instead they have the thickest fur of any animal. A patch the size of your fingertip can hold about as many hairs as a whole human head.

The fur traps a layer of air that keeps cold water away from the skin. That only works if it stays clean and fluffy, so otters spend hours each day grooming, blowing air into their fur and rolling about. A newborn pup's fur holds so much air that the pup can't sink, even if it tries.

Otters also eat a lot. Each day they gulp down about a quarter of their own weight in [[@crabs|crabs]], clams, urchins and other sea creatures, and burning all that food keeps them warm.

Sea otters float on their backs with a flat rock on their chest and smash clams and sea urchins against it. They often keep a favourite rock in a pocket of loose skin under their arm. Pups learn the trick by watching their mothers, and some otters keep using the same rock for days. Along parts of the California coast, otters bashing mussels on the same boulders year after year have left worn, polished patches on the stone. They are among the few mammals apart from humans and other primates that use tools, and they share the habit with clever birds like [[@crow-smart|crows]].

{{story:crow-smart}}

Kelp grows in tall underwater forests along the coasts of California and [[@alaska|Alaska]]. Sea urchins eat kelp. Otters eat sea urchins. In the 1970s, scientists compared islands in Alaska with and without otters. Where otters had disappeared, urchins had chewed whole forests down to bare rock. Where otters lived, the [[@kelp-forests|kelp forests]] were thick and full of fish.

An animal that holds a whole [[habitat|habitat]] together like this is called a [[keystone-species|keystone species]], after the top stone that holds up an arch.

From the 1700s onward, hunters killed sea otters for their fur all along the North Pacific, from Russia to California. By 1911 only a few small groups were left, and an international [[treaty|treaty]] finally protected them. In 1938, people spotted a small group off Big Sur in California, which many had thought was empty of otters. California's otters today descend from them.

They still face dangers. Oil ruins their fur. In 1989, the Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska killed thousands of them. At the Monterey Bay Aquarium, female otters now foster orphaned pups and teach them to dive and use tools before the pups are released into the wild.

India has no sea otters, but it does have river otters. Smooth-coated otters live along rivers like the Chambal and in the [[@mangroves|mangroves]] of the Sundarbans.

text: Yes. Plants can't walk away, but they move all the time. Shoots bend towards light. Roots turn downwards. Climbing stems twist around poles, and many flowers open in the morning and close at night.

Most of these movements are slow, happening by growing more on one side than the other. You would need a [[@cameras-how|camera]] taking a photo every few minutes to see them clearly. Speed the film up, and a bean seedling looks as if it is waving about, searching for something to climb.

A few plants move fast enough to watch. Touch the leaves of the chhui-mui plant, also called lajwanti or touch-me-not, and they fold up within seconds. A Venus flytrap can snap shut on an insect in about a tenth of a second.

sec.h: How a plant moves without muscles
sec.t:
Plants have no [[@muscles|muscles]], so they use water instead. At the base of each chhui-mui leaflet is a small swelling full of water-filled cells. When the leaf is touched, an electrical signal travels through the plant, a bit like a nerve signal. The cells quickly let water out, go floppy, and the leaflets fold.

After a few minutes, the cells fill up again and the leaves slowly open. Scientists think the folding may startle insects and make the plant look less tasty. It works a little like a [[@reflexes|reflex]] in your own body, fast and without thinking.

Slow movements work differently. A shoot bends towards light because cells on its shady side grow longer than cells on its sunny side.

Charles Darwin and his son Francis spent years watching plants move. In 1880 they published a book called *The Power of Movement in Plants*. They showed that a seedling's tip senses light and sends a message down the stem telling it where to bend.

In India, [[@jagadish-bose|Jagadish Chandra Bose]] built a machine called the crescograph in the early 1900s. It magnified a plant's growth thousands of times, so tiny movements could be recorded. Bose showed that plants react to touch, heat, chemicals and injury with electrical signals, much as animal nerves do. Many scientists of his day were doubtful, but later research proved him largely right.

Roots always end up growing downwards, even if you plant a seed upside down. Special cells in the root tip contain heavy grains that settle at the bottom, telling the root which way [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls.

Some plants move to the [[rhythm|rhythm]] of the day. Many [[legume|legumes]] fold their leaves at night, as if asleep. The telegraph plant, found in India, has small side leaflets that jerk around fast enough to see.

In 2014, a team led by Monica Gagliano, working in Australia, dropped potted chhui-mui plants a short, harmless distance again and again. At first, the leaves folded every time. After a while, many plants stopped folding, as if they had learned the drop was harmless. They still folded when touched in other ways.

Some scientists say this shows a simple kind of learning. Others think it may be tiredness or something else, and want more experiments. Either way, plants turn out to be busier than they look, as their [[@seeds-fly|seeds]] show by travelling the world on wind, water and fur.

text: Electricity is made in a power station, usually by spinning a [[generator|generator]]. Its voltage is raised very high so it can travel a long way without losing much energy. Tall steel towers carry it across the country. Near towns, substations lower the voltage step by step. A transformer near your street lowers it one last time, and a cable brings it through your meter and into your switchboard.

All of this happens almost instantly. When you switch on a light, a power station somewhere is already turning a little harder to supply it. Control rooms in each region watch the demand every minute. On a hot evening, when millions of air conditioners and fans come on together, they ask more power stations to join in.

st.prompt: Why do power lines between cities carry electricity at hundreds of thousands of volts, when your home uses only 230?

options.t: High voltage wastes less power over long distances
High voltage makes the electricity travel faster
High voltage keeps birds off the wires

st.reveal: When the same power is sent at a higher voltage, a smaller current flows. Less current means the wires heat up less, so far less energy is lost on the way. Transformers then lower the voltage before it reaches you.

sec.t:
Most power stations spin a [[turbine|turbine]] connected to a generator. The turbine might be pushed by steam from burning coal, by falling water at a [[@dams-power|dam]], or by wind. [[@solar-panels|Solar panels]] are different: they turn sunlight into electricity directly, with nothing spinning.

In India, roughly 70% of electricity still comes from coal (2024). Solar and wind are growing fast. By 2025, about half of India's power-plant capacity was from sources that don't burn [[fossil|fossil]] fuels, such as solar, wind, hydro and nuclear. In the USA, natural gas is the biggest source.

As the power gets close to where people live, substations lower the voltage, first to tens of thousands of volts, then to about 11,000. These are the lines you see on concrete or wooden poles along roads.

The last step is the transformer, a grey metal box on a pole or on the ground near your street. It lowers the voltage to 230 volts for Indian homes. In the USA, homes get 120 volts, which is why some foreign gadgets need an adapter. The current also flips direction back and forth: 50 times a second in India, 60 in America.

The cable from the street goes first to your meter, which counts how many units you use. A unit is one kilowatt-hour: enough to run a ceiling fan for about 12 hours. Then the cable reaches a board of [[@fuses-switches|fuses or circuit breakers]]. Each one guards a different [[circuit|circuit]], such as the kitchen or the bedrooms, and cuts the power if something goes wrong.

From there, copper wires hidden in the walls run to every socket and switch. Grown-ups should handle anything inside them. A switch simply opens or closes a gap in the wire. When you press it, the circuit is complete, and the whole chain, all the way back to that distant turbine, is connected to your lamp.

Public power supply was still new then. In New York, Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station had started selling electricity in 1882. In 1902, a [[hydroelectric|hydroelectric]] station at Shivanasamudra Falls on the Kaveri began sending power about 150 km to the Kolar Gold Fields. It was one of the first big hydro plants in Asia. In 1905, the same plant helped [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] light its streets with electric lamps, years before many other cities in India.

text: Sand artists use the same grains you find on a beach, but in very different ways. Sand sculptors pack wet sand into huge blocks and carve them, like stone. Sand painters pour coloured sand in thin streams to draw on the ground. Sand animators sprinkle sand on a lit glass table and push it around with their fingers, making pictures that change in front of an audience.
What links them is control. A grain of [[@sand-where|sand]] is tiny and hard to steer, so the artist has to learn exactly how it flows, packs and falls.

sec.t:
Dry sand pours like water. Add a little water and something odd happens. A thin film clings to each grain, and where two grains touch, the water forms a tiny bridge that pulls them together. Millions of bridges make the sand stiff enough to carve.

Scientists tested this in 2012 and found sand works best with just a little water, around 1 part in 100. The ancient Egyptians may have known a similar trick. A 2014 study suggested that wetting the sand in front of a sledge halved the force needed to drag a heavy stone, which may help explain how the [[@pyramids|pyramids]] were built.

Some sand art is meant to be destroyed. Tibetan Buddhist monks make sand mandalas, circular designs packed with symbols, by tapping coloured sand through thin metal funnels, a few grains at a time. A large mandala can take a team several days or even weeks.

When it is done, the monks sweep it away and pour the sand into flowing water. The ceremony is a reminder of a teaching of the [[@buddha|Buddha]]: that nothing lasts forever.

In the American Southwest, Navajo healers make sandpaintings from coloured sand, crushed rock and charcoal as part of healing ceremonies. The painting is wiped away afterwards. Families in the [[@navajo-nation|Navajo Nation]] treat these designs as sacred, and photographs of real ceremonial paintings are usually not allowed.

Sand animation is a newer art. The artist works on a glass table lit from below. Where sand is thick, the light is blocked and the glass looks dark. Where the artist sweeps sand away, light shines through. A camera projects the picture on a big screen, and one scene melts into the next.

In 2009, a Ukrainian sand artist told a war story this way on a TV talent show, and the video was watched by millions online.

Indian homes have their own floor art. Many families draw [[@rangoli-art|rangoli]] or kolam each morning with rice flour, coloured powder or sand, letting it trickle through their fingers into patterns of lines and dots. Footsteps and wind wipe it away by evening, and the next morning it starts again. The rice flour has a second job too: ants and birds eat it, so a kolam feeds small creatures as well as decorating the door.

text: Jadav Payeng did it the slow way: one seedling at a time, every day, for more than 40 years. In 1979, when he was about 16, he began planting bamboo on a bare, sandy island in the [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] river in Assam. Then he planted trees. He watered them, protected them and kept going, mostly by himself.

That sandbank is now a forest of about 550 hectares, bigger than Central Park in New York. People call it Molai forest, after his nickname. Rhinos, deer, wild boar and even tigers live there, and wild elephants pass through every year. Jadav Payeng is known across the world as the Forest Man of India.

st.reveal: He began with bamboo, which grows fast and holds sandy soil together. Once it took hold, he planted trees, and the forest slowly began to look after itself.

sec.t:
The Brahmaputra is wide and powerful, and its floods shift sand and soil every year. In 1979, after a big flood, Payeng found many snakes dead on a sandbank near his home. There were no trees to give shade, and the sun had baked them.

He asked village elders what could be done. They told him that only trees could bring the island back to life. So he started, with bamboo first, because it grows quickly and its roots hold loose sand together.

In 2008 forest officials were chasing a herd of about 100 wild elephants that had damaged village crops. The herd vanished into a thick forest that wasn't on any map. That's how officials met Jadav Payeng and saw what he had built.

Since then, Molai forest has become home to animals that need space and cover. Bengal tigers have been seen there, as have one-horned [[@rhino-kaziranga|rhinos]], the kind famous in nearby Kaziranga. Vultures and many other birds nest in its trees.

The Brahmaputra carries a huge load of sand and silt down from the Himalayas. Its channels shift almost every year, swallowing fields in one place and building new sandbanks, called chapori, in another. Families in Assam often lose homes and farmland to the river.

Roots hold soft ground together, slow down floodwater and trap fresh silt. A sandbank covered in trees and grass is much harder for the river to wash away than a bare one, and Payeng's forest has come through many [[monsoon|monsoon]] floods.

Living next to a forest isn't always easy, though. Elephants that shelter there sometimes raid crops and damage houses, and some villagers have asked for trees to be cut. Payeng argues that the animals need the forest, and that without it they would wander even further into farms.

A short film called *Forest Man*, made in 2013, carried his story around the world. In 2015 India gave him the Padma Shri, one of its highest honours. He has been invited to speak to students in many countries.

Payeng still lives simply, keeping cows and selling milk, and he keeps planting. [[erosion|Erosion]] by the river is a big worry in Assam: nearby [[@majuli|Majuli]], the great river island, has lost much of its land over the past century.

He isn't alone in this kind of quiet, stubborn work. In Karnataka, a woman who couldn't have children of her own raised hundreds of banyan trees along a highway, and her story is told in the life of [[@india-tree-mother|Saalumarada Thimmakka]].

text: Computers store everything as long strings of [[@number-zero-one|0s and 1s]], a system called [[binary|binary]]. Each tiny switch in a computer chip is either off, meaning 0, or on, meaning 1. To make this work, you need two things that took humans a very long time to invent: a symbol for nothing, and the idea that a digit's value depends on its place.

Both of these came together in India about 1,500 years ago. Indian mathematicians used a place-value system with zero as a real number. That system travelled to the Arab world and then to Europe. Centuries later, it made binary, and so modern [[@computers-how|computers]], possible.

st.prompt: In binary, which uses only 0 and 1, how would you write the number 4?
st.reveal: In binary, each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. So 100 means one 4, no 2s and no 1s. The zeros hold the empty places, exactly as they do in 400.

sec.t:
Look at the numbers 31, 301 and 3,001. The digits 3 and 1 are the same in each, but the values are completely different. Zero tells you which places are empty. Without it, you would struggle to tell them apart.

Many ancient peoples counted without a proper zero. The Romans wrote 301 as CCCI, with no need to mark empty places, but their [[@roman-numerals|numerals]] made sums slow and clumsy. The Babylonians used a gap or a mark as a placeholder, and the Maya had a zero for their [[@calendars|calendars]].

Indian mathematicians went further. They treated zero as a number in its own right. In 628 CE, Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with it: a number plus zero stays the same, and a number times zero is zero. An [[inscription|inscription]] from 876 CE at the Chaturbhuj temple in Gwalior shows a small round zero in the number 270, carved in stone.

The Bakhshali [[manuscript|manuscript]], found in 1881 near Peshawar and now in Oxford, uses a dot for zero. Carbon dating in 2017 suggested some of its pages are much older than others, and scholars still debate exactly how old the text is.

From India, the system passed to scholars in Baghdad, such as al-Khwarizmi, in the 800s. In 1202, the Italian mathematician Fibonacci explained these "Hindu-Arabic numerals" in a book that helped spread them across Europe.

{{story:binary-code}}

Our everyday system uses ten digits, 0 to 9, perhaps because we have ten fingers. But place value works with any number of digits. In 1703, the German thinker Gottfried Leibniz published an explanation of binary, which uses only two.

In binary, each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. So 101 means one 4, no 2s and one 1, making 5. The zero is essential: it is what makes 101 different from 11. Leibniz admired how simple it was, but in his time it had little practical use.

Long before Leibniz, the Sanskrit scholar Pingala, writing about poetry, described patterns of short and long [[syllable|syllables]]. Some historians point out that his method of listing them works much like binary counting.

Binary became useful when people built machines with switches. A switch has two states, off and on, a perfect match for 0 and 1. In the 1930s and 1940s, engineers began building electronic computers that used binary, together with George Boole's rules of [[@logic|logic]].

Today a single phone chip contains billions of tiny switches called [[transistor|transistors]], each flipping between 0 and 1 billions of times a second. A photo is stored as millions of numbers for the colours of its dots. A song is a long list of numbers describing a sound wave. All of it is written in 0s and 1s, a modern use of the symbol Brahmagupta treated as a number nearly 1,400 years ago.

text: Fast solvers don't work it out from scratch each time. They learn a method that breaks the puzzle into stages, and for each stage they memorise short move sequences, called [[@algorithms|algorithms]]. Then they practise until their fingers do the moves without thinking.

Top "speedcubers" know well over a hundred of these sequences. Before each solve they get 15 seconds to look at the scrambled cube and plan the first steps. They use special cubes that turn smoothly, often with tiny magnets inside. The best solve one in under three seconds.

st.prompt: A scrambled cube can be in about 43 quintillion positions. What is the most moves any of them needs to be solved?

options.t: About 1,000
About a million

st.reveal: Every position can be solved in 20 moves or fewer. A team proved it in 2010 using a huge amount of computer time donated by Google. Fans call this "God's Number", because only a perfect solver could always find the shortest path.

d.try: Turn one face of a solved cube, then turn the next face, and write each move down. Now try to undo the moves in reverse order. You have just used the same idea speedcubers use: every sequence of moves can be run backwards.
myth: You need to be a maths genius to solve a Rubik's Cube.
Most people can learn a beginner's method in a few days. It uses a handful of memorised move sequences and lots of practice. Many children solve the cube in under a minute.

sec.h: A puzzle that began as a lesson
sec.t:
Ernő Rubik was a young [[architecture|architecture]] teacher in Budapest, Hungary. In 1974 he built a cube of wooden blocks held together by a clever hidden core, so each face could turn without the whole thing falling apart. He made it to help his students think about shapes in three dimensions.

Then he scrambled it, and couldn't get it back. It took him about a month. The "Magic Cube" went on sale in Hungary in 1977, and from 1980 a US toy company sold it worldwide as the Rubik's Cube. Hundreds of millions have been sold since.

The most popular fast method is often called CFOP, after its four stages: Cross, First two layers, Orientation and Permutation. You first make a cross on one face, then fill in the first two layers, then fix the top layer in two steps.

The last two steps are where memory matters. There are 57 cases for orienting the top layer and 21 for arranging it, and serious cubers learn a sequence for each. Many top solvers trained by solving thousands of times, a bit like a bowler practising one delivery in the nets until it becomes automatic.

The original cube was stiff and tended to jam. Speed cubes are built differently. Their pieces have rounded edges so a face can turn even when it is slightly out of line, and solvers add silicone lubricant to make them glide. Many now have small magnets that click each layer gently into place.

Solvers also learn "finger tricks": flicking a face with one fingertip instead of gripping and twisting with the whole hand. Watch a [[@how-cameras-speed|slow-motion video]] of a top solve and the hands barely seem to move. The cube's neat [[@symmetry|symmetry]] helps too, because a move sequence learned for one face works the same way on any other.

The World Cube Association runs official contests around the world, including many in India and the USA. Judges scramble the cubes by computer so nobody gets an easy one. Results usually take the average of several solves, so a lucky single doesn't decide the winner.

Records keep falling. In 2023 the American cuber Max Park set a single-solve record of 3.13 seconds. In February 2026, a nine-year-old from Poland, Teodor Zajder, became the first to go under three seconds, with 2.76.

Cubers also race on bigger cubes, up to 7×7, and on oddly shaped cousins. Some solve with one hand, and some blindfolded. A blindfolded solver studies the cube, puts on the mask, and solves it entirely from [[@memory|memory]].

text: Your body is full of strange true facts. You were born with about 300 bones but now have fewer. You shrink a little each day and grow back each night. There is a hole in your vision you never notice. Your body gives off about as much heat as an old 100-watt light bulb, and you share it with trillions of tiny passengers.

None of this is harmful. It is just how bodies work. Many of these oddities are leftovers from our animal ancestors, or clever tricks the body uses to keep running smoothly. Here are some of the weirdest.

st.prompt: A newborn baby has about 300 bones. An adult has 206. Where do the missing bones go?

options.t: Many small bones join together as the baby grows
The body slowly dissolves the extra bones
They fall out like baby teeth

st.reveal: A baby's skeleton has many separate pieces, partly made of soft cartilage. As children grow, some pieces fuse into one. The skull, for example, starts as several plates with soft gaps and slowly joins up.

Brain scans show that we use virtually all of our brain, though not every part at the same moment. Even during sleep, many areas stay busy. The 10% idea has no scientific basis.

sec.t:
Between the bones of your spine sit soft, spongy discs, a bit like jelly-filled cushions. During the day, standing and walking squash them slightly. At night, lying flat, they soak up fluid and puff up again. That's why most people are about a centimetre taller in the morning.

In [[@space-body|space]], there's no [[gravity|gravity]] pressing down at all. NASA has found that astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller, several centimetres, while they are in [[orbit|orbit]]. Spacesuits are made with extra room for this. When they return to Earth, they shrink back.

sec.h: A blind spot in each eye
sec.t:
At the back of each eye, all the nerve fibres bundle together and leave for the brain. That spot has no light [[sensor|sensors]] at all, so you can't see anything that falls on it. Yet you never see a hole in the world. Your brain quietly fills the gap using what's around it and what the other eye sees.

You also blink around 15 to 20 times a minute. Your brain hides those blinks too, so the world doesn't keep going dark.

sec.h: Two metres of DNA in every cell
sec.t:
Almost every cell in your body holds a full copy of your [[@dna|DNA]], the chemical instructions for building you. Unwound and stretched out, the DNA in one cell would be about 2 metres long, taller than a door. It fits because it is wound tightly around tiny [[protein|protein]] spools, like thread on bobbins.

You have trillions of cells, so all your DNA together would be unimaginably long. Your heart helps feed all those cells, beating about 100,000 times a day.

Scientists estimated in 2016 that an average adult carries about 38 trillion [[bacteria|bacteria]], most of them in the gut. That is roughly the same number as human cells in the body, about 30 trillion. Most of these [[@gross-body-bacteria|bacteria]] help, by digesting food and keeping harmful germs out.

In 2009, scientists in Japan used super-sensitive cameras to show that the human body gives off a very faint light. It is about a thousand times too weak for our eyes to see, and it comes from chemical reactions in skin cells. The face glowed most, and the glow changed through the day. And the strangest part? Deep in the ocean, many animals make light bright enough to hunt with, a trick called [[@bioluminescence|bioluminescence]].

text: No. Most germs, or [[microbe|microbes]] as scientists call them, are harmless, and many are helpful. Microbes are living things too small to see without a [[microscope|microscope]]. They include [[bacteria|bacteria]], yeasts and other tiny organisms.

Only a small share of microbes make people ill. Many more live quietly in your gut, on your skin and in your mouth. Together they are called your microbiome. They help you digest food, make some [[@vitamins|vitamins]] and crowd out harmful germs.
Outside your body, microbes make [[@soil-made|soil]] [[fertile|fertile]], put oxygen in the air and turn milk into [[@curd-yogurt|curd]].

options.t: Bacteria from a spoonful of old curd
The milk going stale in the heat
A chemical in the steel bowl

st.reveal: A spoonful of old curd carries live Lactobacillus bacteria. They eat the sugar in milk and make lactic acid, which makes the milk thicken and turn sour. Every bowl of curd is a colony of trillions of helpful bacteria.

myth: Bacteria in your body outnumber your own cells by ten to one.
That figure came from a rough guess in the 1970s. A careful study in 2016 estimated about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells in an average adult, roughly one to one.

sec.t:
Most of your microbes live in your large intestine, the last part of your gut. An adult carries about 38 trillion bacteria there and elsewhere, weighing roughly 200 grams, about as much as a mango.

These [[@digestion-gut|gut bacteria]] eat parts of your food that [[@stomach-digest|your stomach]] and small intestine can't break down, such as some kinds of fibre. In return, they make useful substances, including [[vitamin|vitamin]] K, which helps your blood clot. A rich mix of gut bacteria also seems to help train your [[immune-system|immune system]], so it learns not to attack everything it meets.

A baby in the womb has very few microbes. During and after birth, it picks up bacteria from its mother, from milk, from people who hold it and from everything it puts in its mouth. Within a few years, a child's microbiome looks much like an adult's.

Your microbiome is a bit like a fingerprint. No two people have exactly the same mix, and it shifts with what you eat and where you live.

Indian kitchens have used microbes for thousands of years, without anyone knowing they were there. Curd is milk thickened by bacteria. [[@dosa-idli|Idli and dosa batter]] rises overnight because microbes make gas inside it. [[@food-science-bread-rise|Bread rises]] because of [[yeast|yeast]], which is a tiny fungus. [[@food-why-cheese-holes|Cheese]], vinegar, [[@pickles-achar|pickles]] and soy sauce all depend on microbes too.

{{story:fermentation}}

In fields, bacteria living in the roots of peas, beans and [[@lentils-world|lentils]] take nitrogen from the air and turn it into plant food. Other microbes rot fallen leaves and dead animals, returning their goodness to the soil.

In the oceans, tiny microbes make a large share of the oxygen we breathe. Inside the guts of cows, microbes digest tough grass. Termites rely on microbes in their guts to break down wood, which is why they can eat a wooden door.

People now put microbes to work on purpose. Many [[@antibiotics|antibiotics]] are made by microbes that live in soil, which use them to fight off rival bacteria. Since the 1980s, people with diabetes have used human insulin made by bacteria that scientists gave the human insulin gene. Before that, insulin had to be collected from the bodies of pigs and cattle.

sec.h: The first person to see them
sec.t:
In the 1670s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth seller in Delft in the Netherlands, made tiny but powerful lenses. Looking at drops of water through one of [[@microscopes|his microscopes]], and later at scrapings from his own teeth, he saw "little animals" wriggling about. He was the first person known to see bacteria.

It took another two centuries before scientists proved that some microbes cause disease. That discovery led to soap campaigns, vaccines and new medicines. But it also gave germs a bad name that most of them don't deserve.

text: Hackers who break in usually look for the easiest way through. Often that is a person. They send fake messages, called phishing, that trick someone into typing a password into a fake website. Or they guess weak passwords, or slip in through software that hasn't been updated.

Cybersecurity is the work of keeping computers, phones and networks safe from these attacks. For ordinary people, a few habits block most attacks: keep devices updated, use long and different [[@passwords|passwords]], turn on two-step login, and stop and think before clicking links.

st.prompt: Security experts say one simple step blocks the vast majority of attempts to break into online accounts. Which one?

options.t: Changing your password every day
Turning on two-step login, so a code is also needed
Never using the internet after dark

st.reveal: With two-step login, a stolen password alone is not enough. The attacker also needs a code from your phone or a security key. Companies such as Microsoft and Google report that it stops most automated account attacks.

sec.t:
[[@tech-spam-email|Phishing]] gets its name from "fishing": the attacker throws out bait and waits for a bite. A message might look as if it is from a bank, a delivery company or even a school. It says something urgent, like "Your account will be closed today". The link leads to a fake page that looks just like the real one.

This kind of trickery is called social engineering. It works because people are busy, helpful and sometimes scared. That is why the best defence is often simply to slow down and check.

One of the first big internet attacks was an accident, at least partly. In November 1988 Robert Morris, a student at Cornell University, released a program meant to spread quietly and count how many computers were online. A mistake made it copy itself again and again. Thousands of computers slowed to a crawl or crashed.

Morris became the first person convicted under a new US computer crime law. He later became a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. A floppy disk holding the worm's code is now kept at the Computer History Museum in California.

Defenders use many layers, like a castle with walls, gates and guards. Firewalls filter traffic coming into a network. Antivirus software looks for known bad programs. [[@encryption|Encryption]] scrambles data so stolen files can't be read.

Companies also hire ethical hackers, people paid to try breaking in so holes can be fixed first. Many firms run "bug bounty" programmes that reward anyone who reports a security flaw responsibly. Some teenagers have earned money this way.

Every country now has teams that respond to cyber attacks. In India, CERT-In, part of the Ministry of Electronics and IT, warns about new threats. If someone is cheated online, they can call the national helpline 1930 or report it on the government's cybercrime website. In the USA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency plays a similar role.

If anything online ever feels wrong, such as a scary message or a request for money or passwords, tell a parent or teacher straight away. Good [[@online-safety|online safety]] is mostly about asking before acting.

text: The World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist working at CERN, a big physics laboratory near Geneva in [[@switzerland|Switzerland]].

In 1989, he proposed a way for scientists to share documents by linking them together across [[@internet-history|the internet]]. By the end of 1990, he had written the first web browser, the first web server and the first web pages. He created three key ideas still used today: web addresses (URLs), the language for writing pages (HTML), and the rules computers use to send pages to each other (HTTP).
The internet already existed. Berners-Lee's invention made it easy for anyone to publish and explore information on it.

st.prompt: Which came first, the internet or the World Wide Web?

options.t: The internet, by about 20 years
The web, by about 20 years
They were invented on the same day

st.reveal: The internet grew from networks built in the late 1960s and 1970s. The web came along in 1989 to 1991 as a way to share linked pages over the internet. The internet is the roads; the web is one kind of traffic on them.

The internet is the worldwide network of connected computers and cables. The web is a system of linked pages that runs on top of it. Email, video calls and many apps use the internet without using the web.

sec.h: A lab full of lost information
sec.t:
CERN brings together thousands of scientists from many countries. In the 1980s, they used many kinds of computers, which often couldn't share files. Information got lost, and people had to keep asking each other where things were.

Berners-Lee wanted a system where any document could link to any other, on any computer. In March 1989, he wrote a proposal called "Information Management: A Proposal". His boss, Mike Sendall, wrote "Vague but exciting" on the front and let him keep working on it.

On 30 April 1993, CERN announced that the web's software would be free for anyone to use, with no fees. This decision mattered enormously. Companies, universities and ordinary people could build websites and browsers without asking permission or paying.

The same year, a browser called Mosaic, made at the University of Illinois, showed pictures and text together on the same page and was easy to use. The web began to spread fast beyond science labs.

People often mix up the web and [[@internet-how|the internet]]. The internet is the physical network: cables, routers and computers linked around the world, which grew from the late 1960s. The web is one way of using it, made of pages joined by links.

Before the web, people used the internet for [[@email|email]] and file sharing, mostly with typed commands. The web made it point-and-click. It's a bit like how the [[@printing-press|printing press]] didn't invent writing but made it far easier to share.

There are now more than a billion websites, though many are inactive. To find anything among them, people rely on [[@search-engines|search engines]].

In 1994, Berners-Lee founded the World Wide Web Consortium, which still agrees on standards so websites work on every browser and device. He was knighted in 2004 and has campaigned for the web to stay open to everyone, and for people to have control over their own data. At the [[@olympics-host|2012 London Olympics]] opening ceremony, he appeared at a computer, and a message appeared in lights around the stadium: "This is for everyone".

text: India has a long line of women scientists and engineers, though many of their names are less known than they should be. Anandibai Joshi became one of the first Indian women to earn a medical degree, in 1886. Kamala Sohonie forced her way into research and became a leading biochemist. E. K. Janaki Ammal helped breed better sugarcane. Anna Mani built weather instruments for the whole country.
In recent decades, women have led missile and space projects. Tessy Thomas headed work on long-range Agni missiles, and Muthayya Vanitha and Ritu Karidhal led the Chandrayaan-2 mission to the Moon.

myth: Indian women only began working in science and technology recently.

Indian women were earning medical degrees in the 1880s and doing research in physics, chemistry and botany by the 1930s and 1940s. They often worked against rules and attitudes that tried to keep them out.

sec.t:
Anandibai Joshi was married at nine and became a mother at 14. Her baby died within days, partly for lack of medical care. She decided to become a doctor. In 1883 she sailed to the US and studied at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, graduating in 1886. She fell ill with tuberculosis and died in 1887, aged 21, before she could practise for long. Her courage inspired many.

Around the same time, Kadambini Ganguly in Kolkata became one of the first women in India to graduate in medicine and went on to practise for decades.

In 1933, Kamala Sohonie applied to the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. Its director, the Nobel-winning physicist C. V. Raman, at first refused to admit women. She protested and was allowed in on probation. She passed with distinction, and the next year the institute began accepting more women.

She went on to Cambridge, and in 1939 she earned a PhD in biochemistry. Back in India, she studied the [[nutrition|nutrition]] in foods like neera, a drink made from palm sap, and her work helped improve diets for poor children.

E. K. Janaki Ammal, from Kerala, earned a PhD in botany at the University of Michigan in 1931. At the Sugarcane Breeding Institute in Coimbatore, she helped create varieties suited to Indian conditions, helping India grow more of its own [[@sugar|sugar]].

{{story:maths-history-women}}

Anna Mani studied physics with C. V. Raman. In 1948, she joined the India Meteorological Department, the [[@imd|IMD]]. At the time, India imported almost all its weather instruments. Anna Mani led a workshop that designed and built them in India, from rain gauges to tools for measuring sunlight and [[ozone|ozone]]. She later mapped wind and solar energy across India, long before [[renewable|renewable]] energy was popular.

Tessy Thomas, an engineer from Kerala, joined the Defence Research and Development Organisation and worked on India's Agni missiles. She was project director for Agni-IV, first successfully tested in 2011, and the newspapers called her "Agni Putri". She is often called the first woman to head a missile project in India.

At ISRO, women have played big roles in recent missions. For [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-2]], launched in 2019, Muthayya Vanitha was project director and Ritu Karidhal was mission director. In 2014, photos of women scientists celebrating India's Mars Orbiter reaching Mars were shared around the world.

sec.h: Still a long way to go
sec.t:
Women make up a large share of science students at Indian universities, but far fewer reach senior research jobs. Many leave after marriage or children, or face bias at work. Programmes now offer fellowships to help women return to research after a break.

Astronaut [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]], born in Karnal, flew to space on NASA missions in 1997 and 2003. As a girl she watched small planes at the local flying club, and she went on to study aerospace engineering in Chandigarh and the US. She died in 2003 when the shuttle Columbia broke apart on its return, and India named a weather satellite after her.

text: Jaisalmer is built almost entirely from one kind of rock: a yellow sandstone dug from the desert around it. Houses, temples, mansions and the great fort on the hill are all the same warm colour. In the morning the city looks pale yellow. At sunset it glows like honey, and that is why people call it the Golden City.

The fort is called Sonar Qila, the Golden Fort. Rawal Jaisal, a Bhati Rajput ruler, founded it in 1156 on a hill called Trikuta. More than 850 years later, a few thousand people still live inside its walls.

st.reveal: The fort is built from local yellow sandstone. When the sun is low, its light passes through more air and turns warmer and redder, and the stone glows deep gold.

A few thousand people still live inside it, in houses that families have kept for generations. That makes it one of the world's very few living forts, and also one of the hardest to protect.

sec.h: A fort with people in it
sec.t:
Most old forts are quiet places full of tourists. Jaisalmer's fort has narrow lanes, cows, shops, small hotels, Jain temples from the 12th to 15th centuries and families who have lived there for generations. Its walls have 99 bastions, round towers that let guards see across the sand.

Living forts face a modern problem. Water from taps and drains seeps into the hill, and the soft rock underneath can crumble. Parts of the walls have collapsed after heavy rain. In a city that usually gets under 200 mm of rain a year, while Mumbai gets more than ten times that, the buildings were never designed for much water.

Jaisalmer sat on the [[caravan|caravan]] routes linking India with Persia, Arabia and Central Asia, branches of the old [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] network. Long lines of [[@camels|camels]] carried spices, silk, opium and cloth across the desert, and the city taxed them as they passed.

The traders grew rich and built havelis, tall mansions with stone carved as finely as lace. Patwon ki Haveli is a cluster of five mansions begun in 1805 by a merchant named Guman Chand Patwa. Its windows, called jharokhas, have carved stone screens. These let in breeze and light while keeping out the harsh sun.

Then trade moved to the sea. Once ships sailed from Bombay, caravans faded, and after the border was drawn in 1947 the old routes west were cut. Jaisalmer grew quiet for decades.

{{story:thar-formed}}

The sandstone here formed from sand and mud laid down when parts of this region lay near an ancient sea, many millions of years ago. Not far from the city, at Akal, lie [[fossil|fossil]] tree trunks thought to be about 180 million years old. They grew in forests at a time when dinosaurs walked the Earth, in a place that is now a [[@thar-formed|desert]].

So when you touch a Jaisalmer wall, you touch rock that formed long before the Himalaya even began to rise.

In 1974, the director [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]] made a children's detective film called Sonar Kella, "The Golden Fortress". In it, a boy remembers a past life in a golden fort, and the hero Feluda hunts for it across Rajasthan. Crowds of Bengali visitors still arrive asking for the fort from the film.

Today the city lives on tourism. The Sam sand dunes, about 40 km away, roll in waves several metres high, and every winter there is a Desert Festival with camel races and folk music.

Desert cities live or die by water. Jaisalmer's rulers built Gadisar Lake in the 14th century, a large tank that once held the whole city's water supply. Today the Indira Gandhi Canal carries Himalayan river water hundreds of kilometres into the Thar. Before canals, towns like this depended on clever tanks and deep [[@stepwells|stepwells]], some cut so deep that people climbed down many storeys to reach the water.

text: When a language disappears, its words, songs, stories, jokes and ways of describing the world go with it. Many small languages hold knowledge found nowhere else, such as names for local plants and animals, or ways of reading the weather.

A language usually doesn't vanish suddenly. It fades when children stop learning it. Parents may switch to a bigger language for school, jobs or safety. The grandparents still speak the old language, then only a few elders, then nobody. Of the world's roughly 7,000 languages, a large share are now in danger.

Some languages have been brought back from very few speakers, or even from old records. Hebrew is the best-known example, and Hawaiian, Cornish and the Myaamia language of the US are being revived too.
facts: roughly 40% of them, by some estimates

sec.t:
The Andaman Islands were once home to about ten Great Andamanese languages. After outsiders arrived in the 1800s, disease and violence greatly reduced the islanders' numbers.

Boa Sr was born around 1925 and was the last speaker of Bo. For years, she had nobody to speak her mother tongue with. Linguists recorded some of her words and songs. When she died in January 2010, [[@people-languages-dying|Bo fell silent]]. Some Great Andamanese languages still survive, spoken by a small community in the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]].

India has hundreds of languages, many spoken by small tribal communities. UNESCO's 2009 atlas listed about 197 [[endangered|endangered]] languages in India, more than any other country. Some have no written form, so if speakers stop using them, they leave almost no trace.

Languages are not lost because they are simple or weak. Every language is complex. They fade because of pressure.

Children may be taught only in a national or global language at school. Families move to cities for work. Radio, television and [[@internet-how|the internet]] use bigger languages. In some countries, children were once punished for speaking their own language. In the US, Canada and Australia, Indigenous children were sent to boarding schools where their languages were often banned.

When a community feels its language is old-fashioned or useless, parents may stop passing it on, even out of love, hoping to give children a better start.

{{story:andaman}}

Each language is a different way of seeing. Some languages describe directions using north, south, east and west instead of left and right, even for things on a table. Others have detailed words for kinds of snow, rain or soil.

Local languages often hold knowledge about medicinal plants, fishing grounds or seasonal changes, built up over generations. Linguists compare losing a language to losing a library. It is a little like [[@extinction-today|losing a species]]: something that took thousands of years to grow can disappear in a lifetime.

During the Second World War, the US military used the [[@navajo-nation|Navajo language]] to send coded messages that enemies couldn't break. The [[@code-talkers|code talkers]] showed how valuable a small language could be, even though many of them had been punished as children for speaking it.

Revival is hard but possible. Hebrew had been used for prayer and writing for over 2,000 years but was rarely anyone's first language. From the late 1800s, people began raising children in it, and it now has millions of speakers.

In [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaii]], fewer than 50 children could speak Hawaiian by the early 1980s. Families started "language nest" preschools in 1984, and now there are Hawaiian-medium schools from preschool to university. In Britain, Cornish and Manx have been revived after their last native speakers died.

In India, communities are recording songs, making [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]], and teaching children in their mother tongue in early grades. The UN has named 2022 to 2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages. A language survives when children speak it at play, and every new speaker counts.

text: Breakfast changes almost every few hundred kilometres in India. In the south, people eat steamed idlis, crispy dosas and savoury upma with coconut chutney and sambar. In Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, poha, made from flattened rice, is a favourite. In Punjab, a stuffed paratha with butter and curd is a classic.

These breakfasts grew from what each region grows. Rice-growing areas tend to make rice-based breakfasts, wheat-growing areas make breads, and many dry regions once relied on [[@millets|millets]]. Almost everywhere, the morning starts with a cup of [[@food-chai-history|chai]] or filter coffee.

st.reveal: Overnight, natural yeasts and bacteria eat some of the starch in the rice and urad dal batter. They give off gas, which makes the batter rise and turn slightly sour. Steaming then sets those bubbles into a soft, spongy idli.

sec.h: The south: steamed, fermented and fried
The west: poha, thepla and misal
sec.t:
Poha is flattened rice, made by soaking and pressing rice grains. Rinsed and cooked with onions, mustard seeds, turmeric, [[@peanut-butter|peanuts]] and [[@curry-leaves|curry leaves]], it takes about ten minutes to make. In Indore, it's served with sev, a crunchy gram flour topping, and often with jalebi.

In Maharashtra, misal pav pairs a spicy sprouted-bean curry with soft bread rolls. Gujaratis eat [[@gujarati-food|thepla]], a thin flatbread with fenugreek leaves, which keeps for days and is a favourite for train journeys. On weekends, many families buy fafda, crunchy gram flour strips, from the local shop.

sec.h: The north and east: breads and fried treats
sec.t:
In Punjab, a breakfast paratha might be stuffed with potato, cauliflower, radish or paneer, then cooked on a griddle with ghee and served with white butter and curd. In Delhi, chole bhature, spicy chickpeas with puffy fried bread, is a weekend treat.

Bengalis love luchi, small fried breads made from refined flour, with alur dom, a potato curry. In Bihar, sattu, flour made from roasted gram, is mixed with water as a filling drink on hot mornings. In Rajasthan, people may start the day with a spicy kachori stuffed with lentils or onion.

In the USA, many people eat breakfast cereal with milk. That habit began in the late 1800s, when [[@cereal-history|cereals]] like cornflakes were sold as healthy foods. Today packaged cereals and oats are also common in Indian cities, especially for busy families.

Many people in both countries eat a mix: cornflakes on school days, aloo paratha or dosa on Sunday. Pancakes in America and dosas in India are distant cousins, both thin batters cooked on a hot flat pan.

Most of India starts the day with chai, black tea boiled with milk, sugar and often ginger or cardamom. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, filter coffee is more common, poured from a height between a steel tumbler and a bowl called a dabara to cool and froth it.

In [[@kashmir|Kashmir]], some people drink noon chai, a pink, salty tea. In Ladakh, butter tea, made with salt and butter, gives warmth and energy in the thin, cold air.

text: For many Indian vegetarians, the main reason is [[ahimsa|ahimsa]], the idea of not harming living beings. It is central to [[@jain-agamas|Jainism]] and important in Buddhism and many Hindu traditions. Over centuries it shaped what families cooked, and many kept the habit for generations.

Other reasons play a part too: family custom, caste and community traditions, cost, health and simple taste. But vegetarianism is far from universal. A 2021 survey found that about four in ten Indian adults call themselves vegetarian. The rest eat some meat, fish or eggs, and the mix varies hugely from one state to the next.

sec.t:
Hinduism has no single rule about meat. Some Hindu communities have been strictly vegetarian for centuries, often for religious reasons, while many others eat fish, chicken or mutton. In Bengal, fish is part of many festival meals.

Many Hindus avoid beef because the [[@cows-india|cow]] is treated as sacred, and others avoid meat on certain days of the week or during festivals like Navratri. So one person might be vegetarian on Tuesdays and not on Sundays.

Most Indian vegetarians are lacto-vegetarians. They avoid meat, fish and often eggs, but eat [[@milk|milk]], curd, ghee and paneer. That is different from vegans, who avoid all animal foods.

Indian vegetarian cooking is rich because it had to be. [[protein|Protein]] comes from [[@pulses-dal|pulses]], dairy and nuts. Spices, souring agents and many vegetables keep meals interesting. A [[@gujarati-food|Gujarati]] or Udupi [[@thali|thali]] can hold a dozen dishes without a gram of meat.

Packaged food in India carries a symbol by law: a green dot inside a green square for vegetarian, and a brown mark for non-vegetarian. Visitors are often surprised to see it on biscuits, chips and [[@soft-drinks|soft drinks]]. In the United States, no such mark is required, and vegetarians check ingredient lists instead.

If you coloured a map of India by how many people are vegetarian, it would be patchy. Surveys find the highest shares in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab. Along the coasts and in the east, where rivers and the sea provide plenty of fish, the shares are much lower.

In Kerala, West Bengal, Odisha and most of the Northeast, only a small minority avoid meat and fish. Even within one city, a Marwari family and a Malayali family living next door may eat very differently. Food habits follow history, religion and geography all at once.

About 5% of American adults told Gallup in 2018 that they were vegetarian. In the West, people often give up meat for the environment, animal welfare or health. A young Mohandas [[@gandhi|Gandhi]], studying law in London from 1888, joined the London Vegetarian Society and wrote for its magazine. He found that English vegetarians had very different reasons from his family back in Gujarat, though they ended up at the same dinner table.
